---
title: "R10. Uncertainty, assumptions and limitations"
description: "What uncertainty is, how to manage it, and how to write it up."
---

What the terms mean, and how uncertainty is identified, quantified and communicated.

*Phases 2 and 3. [Phase 2, design](../02-design/index.qmd) and
[Phase 3, analysis](../03-analysis/index.qmd).*

All analysis is uncertain. Identify your uncertainty, manage it, and tell the reader about it in
terms they can act on.

## What uncertainty is

Uncertainty describes the difference between an estimate and the true value. It arises from
measurement and sampling error, how data was collected, and missing data. It also arises from
under-reporting, the assumptions you had to make, and the limits of the method itself.

**Direct uncertainty** is uncertainty about an estimate that can be measured or quantified. It is
communicated in absolute terms: a standard error, a confidence or credible interval, statistical
significance.

**Indirect uncertainty** is uncertainty about the underlying quality of knowledge surrounding an
estimate. It is not directly measured but inferred from the analysis.

Indirect uncertainty is usually communicated as caveats. It can also be summarised on a qualitative
or ordered scale such as [the GRADE scale](https://gdt.gradepro.org/app/handbook/handbook.html). The
GRADE scale grades how much confidence to place in a body of evidence.

Most analysis has both. Report both, not only the one with a number attached.

### Uncertainty in a forecasting model {#uncertainty-in-a-forecasting-model}

Uncertainty is stated beside a forecast, because what the model does not know is most of what the
reader needs. [Communicating it](#communicating-it) sets out how to state it.

## Manage uncertainty at design, not at write-up {#manage-uncertainty-at-design-not-at-write-up}

Address uncertainty during the analytical cycle. That lets you design and plan the analysis
proportionately, and choose your assumptions, options and scenarios.[^src-govs-010-section-6-5]

By the time you are writing up, your options have narrowed to describing the uncertainty you have.
Handled at design, you can choose a method that reduces it.

At design, **search the planned analysis systematically for sources and types of uncertainty**.[^src-aqua-book-section-7-4]
Look for any large enough to breach the acceptable margin of error. Do this while there is still time
to design for them. GovS 010 section 5.3 says the designed approach should consider uncertainty.[^src-govs-010-section-5-3]

You should:[^src-govs-010-section-6-5]

- **identify the sources** of uncertainty and consider their impacts
- **analyse it at the level the decision requires**, and no further
- **develop options for managing it**, and take appropriate control and mitigation actions

## Assumptions

An assumption is something you have taken to be true without establishing it. Every analysis has
them. The failure is not making assumptions, it is leaving them unrecorded.

For each material assumption, record:

| Field | What goes in it |
|---|---|
| The assumption | Stated plainly, so someone else can judge it |
| Rationale | Why it is reasonable |
| Impact if wrong | The direction and rough scale of the error if the assumption fails |
| Sensitivity tested | Yes or no. Testing is first required at Level 2 Enhanced, where material |
| Agreed with | Who accepted it, and when |

: The fields of an assumptions entry and what goes in each

An assumption whose failure would not change the conclusion is worth recording briefly. One whose
failure would reverse the conclusion needs stating in the output itself.

Where you can, **test the sensitivity of your key assumptions**, and plan that testing in Phase 2,
design, rather than retrofitting it. You and the commissioner agree the acceptable margin of error
at scoping, along with the levels of quality and certainty the analysis
needs.[^src-govs-010-section-5-2] Sensitivity testing is how you find out whether an assumption
could push you past it.

[Deciding your assurance level](../07-deciding-your-assurance-level/index.qmd) first requires
sensitivity testing at Level 2 Enhanced, where it is material. Levels 3 and 4 inherit that
requirement.

## Limitations

A limitation is something your analysis cannot do. State them in terms of use, not in terms of
method, because use is what the reader is deciding about.

Take "the data has incomplete coverage for two months". Write "these figures understate activity in
July and August, so they should not be used to compare quarters" instead.

Write a sentence that begins **"this analysis should not be used to..."**, and name the specific
misuse it cannot support.

## Communicating it

When disseminating results, expressions of uncertainty should:[^src-govs-010-section-6-5]

- **be quantitative where possible**
- be balanced, avoiding unwarranted confidence in a particular option

In practice:

- **Be transparent** about uncertainty, to avoid misinterpretation and misuse
- **Be specific** about what exactly is uncertain and why, how it has been quantified, the
  limitations of the data, and the assumptions made
- **Use plain language**, so that what you write about uncertainty can be understood by everyone who
  will read it
- **Show it in your visualisations**, data tables and datasets, and explain what it represents. It is
  not enough to confine it to a quality and methodology annex

For official statistics, Standard 7 of the Code of Practice requires producers to prominently
explain quality, including strengths and limitations. It also requires them to communicate the
uncertainty in estimates. See [which standards apply to you](r8-the-standards-landscape.qmd).
